title: What would you need before letting an AI trading agent touch real funds?
author: Open_Swimming5859
selftext:
Been working on Agon with my team and wanted feedback from people who are actually into AI trading.

The idea is to use a trader’s own history to surface the limits and rules they already tend to follow, then keep the agent operating inside those boundaries.

The important part for us is that the agent shouldn’t be the thing enforcing its own limits.

So even if you switch agents, the guardrails stay with you.

We’re starting with a read-only beta first.

What would you need to see before you’d let an AI trading agent operate with real funds?

Hard spend caps? Approval for every trade? Emergency revoke? Something else?

waitlist.getagon.tech

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
Before real funds, I’d want the read-only beta to show every limit inferred from my trading history, the evidence behind it, and whether I explicitly approved it. History can encode old account sizes or accidental behavior, so it should not silently become policy.

Then run the proposed trades in shadow mode and report which ones the external guardrails blocked. I’d also test emergency revoke during a pending order and confirm that switching agents cannot bypass open-order or daily-loss limits. How are inferred rules promoted into enforced rules?

replies.author: Both-Assistant4859
replies.body: Trail first to iron out the bugs and hone the $$. I am on my third 🤖. Every time increasing outcome. Proof is in tracking. Not taking the stock that one goes 25% always searching for 50 percent or better

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
I agree with all of that, especially treating inferred rules as proposals rather than policy. A few things I'd add. Each promoted rule should carry a version, an owner and an expiry or review date, since account size and strategy change and an old limit can quietly become wrong. I'd also separate hard limits (never exceeded, like max daily loss or max position size) from soft ones that only warn, so a loose inference can't become a hard block by accident.

For shadow mode, track not just how many trades the guardrails blocked but how those trades would have done, so you can tell whether a limit is protecting you or just costing you. And test failure behavior: if the guardrail service is unreachable or times out, the agent should fail closed and place nothing.

Limits tied to scheduled events are another worthwhile category, such as no new entries around CPI, FOMC or earnings for names you hold. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing that a guardrail layer could use for that.

comments.author: SuperOrbital_Trading
comments.body: Apparently not much since I am already about 90% of the way to building an entire hands off trading system for myself.

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
For me the key requirement would be that the agent never has withdrawal permissions and cannot override its own risk limits.

I’d want trade-only access, hard position/exposure caps enforced outside the agent, a one-click emergency revoke, full activity logs and a long read-only/paper phase before touching real funds.

The AI can make decisions, but it shouldn’t be the thing deciding how much authority it has.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
keeping the guardrail outside the agent matters more than anything else on your list, most people get that backwards. for me it'd be a key that can't open anything on its own, only close and cancel, plus a revoke that works from my phone without the agent's cooperation. approval on every trade sounds safe but people stop reading the prompts after a week.

I built Quantradin around the same split. it's free, no real money involved, and a read-only connection there can look and step back (close, cancel, pause) but can never open a trade or switch a bot on. it's at quantradin.com if you want to compare notes.
